source.title: Actionable Interpretability via Causal Hypergraphs: Unravelling Batch Size Effects in Deep Learning
source.authors: Zhong-Tian Sun; Anoushka Harit; Pietro Lio

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and table formatting appear corrupted or flattened, but the batch-size accuracy tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on generalization in graph and text classification tasks, extending the batch-size finding to new domains and models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy across batch sizes for HGCNet and several baselines. Rows below cover HGCNet's separate dataset and batch-size results. It does not report a fixed-epoch comparison or a workload-dependent threshold.
record.test_reason: The study reports batch-size effects on graph and text classification, but uses early stopping and does not establish equal epoch budgets. These results cannot determine V5's fixed-epoch penalty. It tests none of the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: they claim smaller batches causally improve generalization, principally through increased gradient noise and flatter minima. This is their interpretation; equal epoch budgets are not established, and the causal estimates depend on their assumed causal structure.
record.recipe_differences: Batch-size comparisons in graph and text tasks using HGCNet; this is an extension beyond the large-batch image-classification and language-model settings described in V5. Epoch budget is not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and batch size: reported test scores decline as batch size increases across the four datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Tables 2–5 report decreasing HGCNet held-out scores from batch 16 to 512: Cora 83.9→81.5, CiteSeer 79.1→76.8, Amazon 92.4→89.2, and PubMed 88.2→85.1. Equal epoch budgets are not established.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Smaller batches yield higher reported held-out scores in these graph and text classification experiments under the study's training and stopping procedures.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 16 reports increasing largest Hessian eigenvalues with batch size. This is unscaled curvature, without the matched-training-loss, generalization-gap ranking or competing-measure comparisons required by V7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger batches are associated with larger maximum Hessian eigenvalues in the reported graph and text classification runs.

record.problems: The paper does not state the epoch budget or establish that it is fixed across batch sizes. It gives no training-error values for these batch-size comparisons, and the PubMed prose and table caption use inconsistent metric names. The reported causal interpretation relies on a prespecified causal structure and assumptions described in the paper.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2–5 also report the GCN, GAT, BGAT, PI-GNN, GIN, BERT, RoBERTa and DistilBERT batch-size results; omitted to prioritize the HGCNet batch-size series within the row budget. Other batch-size analyses and ablations in Tables 8–17 were not extracted because they were not required to establish the reported batch-size/test-score pattern or concern additional interventions and mediators.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out performance under matched architectures and recipes.
Width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons under specified tuning budgets.

The fixed-epoch large-batch penalty in image classifiers or language models; workload-dependent thresholds; recovery through longer training, warmup, normalization or regularization changes. Early stopping is reported, but equal epoch budgets are not established.
Held-out error with versus without dropout; small-data and excessive-dropout regimes.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, ranking generalization gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, and comparisons against norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The reported batch-size trend has material internal contradictions. Table 13 gives HGCNet batch-512 accuracies of 83.7, 79.3, 88.3 and 92.5, versus batch-16 values of 83.9, 79.1, 88.2 and 92.4, showing near equality or slight improvements on three datasets. Tables 10–14 elsewhere use batch-512 values of 80.5, 76.0, 84.8 and 89.0, differing from Tables 2–5. Table 14's stated mean ATE of +2.4 percentage points also disagrees with its displayed endpoint differences. These inconsistencies require clarification before treating the batch-size effect as robust. Tables 8–17 were explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence were not tested.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold were not tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers were not compared.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization was not tested.

The paper varies batch size and reports held-out accuracy, but does not state or compare a fixed epoch budget, establish a workload-dependent batch threshold, or test the recipe adjustments named in the version.
Dropout's effect on test error was not isolated.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its relation to the training-test gap were not measured.
Removing memorized training examples was not tested.
